Tests dependent through a shared latent variable in simulated data

Source: R/simulate.R
latent_dependence.Rd

latent_dependence() makes the simulated test results dependent given the disease status through one continuous latent variable shared by all the tests of a subject, such as the severity of the condition among the diseased or a condition that causes false positives among the healthy. The sensitivity and specificity of each test do not change: the latent variable changes only how often the tests are right or wrong together. The object is passed to simulate_study() as its dependence argument.

Usage

latent_dependence(diseased_loadings = 0, healthy_loadings = 0)

Arguments

diseased_loadings

Loadings \(b_{1k}\) of the tests among the diseased: a numeric vector of finite values, of any sign, either of length 1 (the same loading for all tests) or of length \(K\) (one loading per test, in the order of the sensitivity argument of simulate_study()). Any combination of finite values is allowed; the Details describe the dependences each combination produces. Default 0: the tests are independent among the diseased. The length is checked against \(K\) when the data are simulated.

healthy_loadings

Loadings \(b_{0k}\) of the tests among the healthy, with the same form as diseased_loadings. Default 0: the tests are independent among the healthy.

Value

An object of class latent_dependence.

Details

Each subject has a latent variable \(Z \sim N(0, 1)\), independent of the disease status \(D\). Given \(D = d\) and \(Z = z\) the \(K\) tests are independent, with $$P(T_k = 1 \mid D = d, Z = z) = \Phi(a_{dk} + b_{dk} z),$$ where \(\Phi\) is the standard normal distribution function and \(b_{dk}\) is the loading of test \(k\) in class \(d\) (diseased_loadings for \(d = 1\), healthy_loadings for \(d = 0\)). The intercepts are $$a_{1k} = \Phi^{-1}(Se_k)\sqrt{1 + b_{1k}^2}, \qquad a_{0k} = \Phi^{-1}(1 - Sp_k)\sqrt{1 + b_{0k}^2},$$ so that, integrating out \(Z\), \(P(T_k = 1 \mid D = 1) = Se_k\) and \(P(T_k = 0 \mid D = 0) = Sp_k\) exactly, for any value of the loadings.

Equivalently, test \(k\) is positive when a normal latent variable \(Y_k = b_{dk} Z + \varepsilon_k\), with \(\varepsilon_k \sim N(0, 1)\) independent, exceeds a threshold. Within class \(d\) the correlation of \(Y_j\) and \(Y_k\) is $$\rho_{d,jk} = \frac{b_{dj}\, b_{dk}}{\sqrt{(1 + b_{dj}^2)(1 + b_{dk}^2)}}.$$ Hence:

  • a loading 0 makes its test independent of all the others in that class;

  • tests \(j\) and \(k\) agree more often than under independence when \(b_{dj} b_{dk} > 0\), and less often when \(b_{dj} b_{dk} < 0\);

  • larger loadings in absolute value give stronger dependence. For example, two tests with sensitivity 0.8 and loadings 1 among the diseased have \(\rho = 0.5\) and an odds ratio of about 4.7 between their results; with loadings 2, \(\rho = 0.8\) and an odds ratio of about 19.

Allowed values. Every combination of finite real values is allowed: the loadings of a class are not constrained by each other, by the loadings of the other class or by the sensitivities and specificities, and every combination gives a valid distribution of the results with the requested sensitivities and specificities. The two classes are independent choices, so everything below holds separately among the diseased and among the healthy.

Dependences that can be obtained. Since all the tests share one latent variable, the loadings cannot produce every pattern of pairwise dependences. Write \(s_k = |b_{dk}| / \sqrt{1 + b_{dk}^2}\), a number in \([0, 1)\) that measures how strongly test \(k\) depends on \(Z\); then \(|\rho_{d,jk}| = s_j s_k\). Hence:

  • strength: each test has a single strength \(s_k\), and the dependence of a pair is the product of the strengths of its two tests. For three tests \(|\rho_{d,23}| = |\rho_{d,12}\, \rho_{d,13}| / s_1^2 \ge |\rho_{d,12}\, \rho_{d,13}|\), so tests 2 and 3 cannot be much less dependent on each other than both are on test 1: for example \(\rho_{d,12} = \rho_{d,13} = 0.8\) forces \(\rho_{d,23} \ge 0.64\). All the correlations are strictly between \(-1\) and 1;

  • sign: the sign of \(\rho_{d,jk}\) is the product of the signs of \(b_{dj}\) and \(b_{dk}\). The tests split into those with positive and those with negative loading, with positive dependence within each group and negative dependence between the groups. Changing the sign of all the loadings of a class gives the same distribution, so only the relative signs matter. For any three tests the product \(\rho_{d,12}\, \rho_{d,13}\, \rho_{d,23}\) is never negative: for example, three tests cannot all be negatively dependent on each other;

  • independence: \(\rho_{d,jk} = 0\) only when \(b_{dj} = 0\) or \(b_{dk} = 0\), and a loading 0 makes its test independent of all the others. Two tests cannot be independent of each other while both depend on a third.

To give the same correlation \(\rho \in [0, 1)\) to every pair, use the same loading \(b = \sqrt{\rho / (1 - \rho)}\) for all tests: \(b = 0.5\) gives \(\rho = 0.2\), \(b = 1\) gives \(\rho = 0.5\) and \(b = 2\) gives \(\rho = 0.8\). Patterns outside these limits, such as a correlation of any sign and size for each pair, are obtained with dependence = probit_dependence(...).

See also

simulate_study(), independence(), probit_dependence(), random_effects(), which fits the same latent structure

Examples

# same loading for all tests among the diseased, independence among the healthy
latent_dependence(diseased_loadings = 1)
#> <latent_dependence> tests dependent through a shared latent variable
#>   diseased_loadings: 1
#>   healthy_loadings: 0

# one loading per test and class: A and B strongly dependent among the
# diseased, C almost independent; among the healthy only A and B, weakly
dep <- latent_dependence(diseased_loadings = c(1, 1, 0.3),
                         healthy_loadings = c(0.5, 0.5, 0))
d <- simulate_study(n = 2000, prevalence = 0.3,
                    sensitivity = c(A = 0.9, B = 0.8, C = 0.7),
                    specificity = c(A = 0.85, B = 0.9, C = 0.95),
                    verification_prob = 1, dependence = dep)
sick <- d$disease == 1
cor(d[sick, c("A", "B", "C")])
#>           A         B         C
#> A 1.0000000 0.2771135 0.1627437
#> B 0.2771135 1.0000000 0.1122374
#> C 0.1627437 0.1122374 1.0000000

# mixed signs: A and B agree, C disagrees with both
latent_dependence(diseased_loadings = c(1, 1, -1))
#> <latent_dependence> tests dependent through a shared latent variable
#>   diseased_loadings:  1,  1, -1
#>   healthy_loadings: 0
